title: Model Photos Without a Photoshoot | AIVideosUGC
description: Get model photos without a photoshoot: photograph the garment flat, describe the model and setting, then check the fit before posting. Learn how and try it.
h1: How to Get Model Photos Without a Photoshoot
lead: Skip the model, photographer, and studio day. Upload a flat lay or hanger photo of your piece and get an on-model image in minutes, for new arrivals, short runs, and print-on-demand. Here's how to prepare the photo, describe the model, and catch the fit details AI can get wrong.
secondary_keywords: on-model photos from a flat lay
summary: How small clothing and jewelry brands can turn flat product photos into on-model images, plus the fit details to look over first.

sections.h2: When AI model photos make sense
paras: A model shoot means booking a person, a photographer, a location, and a day, then waiting for edits. That's hard to justify for a small run of hoodies or a handful of new earrings.

[AI model photos](page:model-photos) fill that gap. You upload a photo of the piece, describe who's wearing it and where, and get an image of it being worn. They're handy for new arrivals, short production runs, print-on-demand designs, and trying out a style before you commit to a full shoot.

They're less suited to showing exact fit. A generated image can't tell a shopper how a medium will sit on their own body, so keep your size chart and measurements in the listing. More ideas for clothing brands are on our [fashion and clothing page](page:ind-fashion-clothing). A [lifestyle product photo](page:lifestyle-photos) can show the same piece in a setting without implying a precise fit.
sections.alt: Adult woman with short copper hair wearing a plain gray hoodie on an autumn city sidewalk.

sections.h2: Photograph the garment so nothing is left to guess
paras: Lay the piece flat on a plain sheet or hang it against a bare wall, and shoot straight on in daylight. Steam out wrinkles first, since creases in your photo can turn into odd folds on the model. Our [product photo guide](page:guide-product-photo-tips) covers lighting and framing.

Get the whole garment in frame, with sleeves, hem, and collar visible. Turn it so the print or logo faces the camera. Photograph each color separately rather than asking for a color change, because a generated color may not match your actual dye.
For jewelry, use a plain surface, get close, and keep the clasp, stones, and chain in sharp focus. With small pieces, a crisp source photo matters more than anything else.
sections.alt: Hands smooth a plain gray hoodie beside a wooden hanger on a light surface.

sections.h2: Describe the model and the setting
paras: One or two sentences is plenty. Cover the person, the pose, the place, and the light. You don't need to describe the clothing in detail, since that comes from your photo. If you'd rather not write anything, the [Clothing Try-On](page:tpl-tryon), [Jewelry On Model](page:tpl-jewel), and [Lookbook](page:tpl-look) templates give you a ready-made starting point.

Some examples. Linen dress: "A woman in her 40s walking along a sunny beach path, relaxed smile, late afternoon light." Hoodie: "A young man leaning on a brick wall on a city street, hands in the front pocket, overcast daylight." Drop earrings: "Close-up of a woman's profile with her hair tucked behind her ear, soft studio light, neutral backdrop."
Use model examples that reflect the sizes and styles you sell, and keep the garment details visible for review. Don't describe a celebrity or ask for a lookalike; those requests may be refused.
sections.alt: Adult Black woman with short natural hair wearing a plain gray hoodie by a brick wall.

sections.h2: Check the fit and the details
paras: Compare each image with the real piece before you use it. Look at the neckline shape, sleeve and hem length, where the print sits, how many buttons there are, and which side the zipper is on. Stripes and checks should line up the way they do on the actual garment.

For jewelry, check the clasp, count the stones, and see whether a necklace falls where it should on the chest for its length. Hands and hairlines deserve a second look as well, since they're common spots for small glitches.

If anything doesn't match, make a new version rather than posting one that's close enough. Then run through [Before You Publish: A Checklist for AI Content](page:blog-ai-video-review-checklist) before the photo goes live.
sections.alt: Adult East Asian man checking the sleeve and hem of a plain gray hoodie in a fitting room.

sections.h2: Build a small set for each piece
paras: For each item, plan two or three images: one full-length or full-view shot, one closer crop that shows the fabric or the stone, and one in a setting that fits how it's worn. Each is a separate request with its credit cost shown first.

When you have a few results, pick the ones that look like they belong together, with similar light and backgrounds, so your listing doesn't jump between styles. The [examples page](page:examples) shows hoodies, handbags and boots followed from the first photo to worn and lifestyle images.
sections.alt: Adult woman with short auburn hair wearing a plain gray hoodie by a leafy park path.

paras: On a [Shopify](page:plat-shopify) or Etsy listing, lead with a clean product shot and follow it with one or two on-model images, so shoppers see both the details and the piece being worn. They come out square by default, a shape that sits neatly in a typical product gallery.

For [Instagram](page:plat-instagram), a few on-model photos in different settings make an easy new-arrivals post. Add the price or a "New in" line afterward in Canva. Everything you make stays private in your account until you decide to post it.
sections.alt: Adult man with short silver hair wearing a plain gray hoodie outside a storefront.

faq.q: Do I need to say the model in my photos is AI-generated?
faq.a: Yes. Check the current disclosure rules for the platform or marketplace where the image will appear. Amazon, TikTok, Meta, and local law can each require different labels; follow the official rule for the site you post to.

faq.q: Will the same model appear in all my photos?
faq.a: No. There is no saved model to reuse, so the person can look different from one photo to the next. Describing age, hair, and build in the same words each time helps the set look related.

faq.q: What source photo works for an AI model photo?
faq.a: Use a sharp, front-facing garment photo with the whole item visible. Smooth wrinkles and use even light so fabric, print, and trim are easier to review.

faq.q: Can an AI model photo prove a garment fits?
faq.a: No. A generated image cannot prove how a size will sit on a shopper, so keep your size chart and measurements in the listing.

faq.q: How many credits does one model photo use?
faq.a: One model photo uses 24 credits, and the exact cost appears before the job starts. Credits for a failed job return to your balance.

faq.q: Can I use jewelry as well as clothing?
faq.a: Yes. Use a close, sharp source photo that shows the clasp, stones, and chain clearly, then check those details in the result.

faq.q: How should I review a generated model photo?
faq.a: Compare it with the real piece before posting. Check the neckline, sleeve and hem length, print position, buttons, zipper side, clasp, stones, hands, and hairline.
